main.t: A butterfly-shaped gland in front of the trachea that makes the hormones that set the metabolic rate.

simpler.t: Your thyroid is a small gland in your neck. Its hormones control how fast your body uses energy.

deeper.t: It makes T3 and T4 from iodine, and calcitonin from its parafollicular cells.

facts.t: It lies in front of the trachea, just below the larynx.
The parathyroid glands are embedded in the back of its lobes.

simpler.t: It sits low in the front of your neck, below your voice box.

deeper.t: Its two lobes wrap round the sides of the trachea, joined by the isthmus in front.
deeper.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the lobes wrap round the sides of the trachea.

items.name: Isthmus
items.t: The narrow middle part that joins the two lobes.

items.name: Lobes
items.t: Wing-shaped right and left lobes either side of the isthmus.

items.name: Follicles
items.t: Hollow spheres of follicle cells filled with colloid, where the hormones are made.

items.name: Parafollicular (C) cells
items.t: Cells between the follicles that make calcitonin.

simpler.t: Two wings joined in the middle, full of tiny hormone-making sacs.

deeper.t: Iodine attaches to thyroglobulin in the colloid to build the hormones.

facts.t: T3 and T4 raise the basal metabolic rate, the energy the body uses at rest.
They are needed for growth, and especially for the developing nervous system.
Thyroid hormone release is controlled by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the pituitary, by negative feedback.

simpler.t: Its hormones turn up the body’s energy use and help children grow.

items.name: Parathyroid glands
items.t: Embedded in the back of its lobes.

items.name: Anterior pituitary
items.t: Releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid.

items.name: Hypothalamus
items.t: Releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), which triggers TSH secretion.

simpler.t: It sits on the windpipe, below the voice box, and is controlled by the pituitary.

facts.t: Its hormones are critical for normal development of the nervous system before birth and in early childhood.
Where diets lack iodine, iodised salt is the main source in many countries.

items.injury: Too little iodine in the diet.
items.damaged: Hormone production in the thyroid follicles.
items.cannotDo: Make T3 and T4: the gland swells into a goitre.
items.why: TSH rises, and colloid builds up in the overstimulated follicles.

items.cannotDo: Keep a normal metabolic rate: they gain weight and feel cold.
items.why: Low T3 and T4 slow the use of energy throughout the body.

items.q: Explain why iodine deficiency causes a goitre.
model: Without iodine, T3 and T4 cannot be made.
Low T3 and T4 remove negative feedback.
Overstimulated follicles store more colloid, and the gland enlarges.

items.q: Compare follicle cells and parafollicular cells.
model: Follicle cells surround the colloid and make T3 and T4.
Their hormones raise the metabolic rate.
Parafollicular cells lie between follicles and make calcitonin.
Calcitonin tends to lower blood calcium.

items.q: Predict the TSH level in someone with low T3 and T4 from thyroid inflammation.
model: Low T3 and T4 reduce negative feedback.

check.why: Parafollicular (C) cells between the follicles make calcitonin.

check.stem: Which hormone stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4?
check.why: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates release.

options: In front of the trachea, below the larynx
check.why: It lies anterior to the trachea, just inferior to the larynx.
